title: Outcomes of Field Studies of Adaptive Birth Sex Allocation in Southern Elephant Seals Differ With Study Site
content:
ABSTRACT

Extreme sexual dimorphism and a polygynous mating system have made elephant seals (Mirounga sp.) attractive candidates for testing predictions of adaptive sex allocation theory in relation to maternal quality in mammals. The birth sex ratio in the southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) was investigated at South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean, and shown to be skewed toward female offspring when mothers weighed less than a threshold mass. However, the authors of that study also suggested more data were needed to confirm and refine their mass threshold estimates. Here we replicated the South Georgia study for a different southern elephant seal population at Macquarie Island, South Indian Ocean. Field observations and measurements for post-partum maternal age, body length, and mass were paired with offspring sex, ensuring comparisons of results could be made between studies. We used two standard and one nonstandard binomial regression approaches to analyze for deviations from unity in the offspring sex ratio in relation to measured maternal variables. Like other studies of elephant seals, we found no evidence for a relationship between offspring sex and maternal age or body length. In contrast to the findings of the South Georgia study, we found no evidence for the existence of post-partum maternal mass thresholds in the Macquarie Island data. Inconsistencies in the outcomes of adaptive sex allocation studies for different populations within the same species are difficult to explain.
